projects.name: AGI_Research
projects.description: Public lab notebook — committed daily since July 2026. Linear algebra, calculus and probability from axioms → neural nets and backprop in pure NumPy (SGD through Adam) → now CNNs, Transformers and PyTorch. No shortcuts.
projects.longDescription:
A public lab notebook committed daily since 1 July 2026 — 548 days to 31 Dec 2027. I derive everything by hand: linear algebra, calculus and probability from axioms, then neural nets, backprop, optimisers from SGD to Adam in pure NumPy, now CNNs and Transformers.

Each day is a notebook with math, code and reflection — no autograd, no shortcuts. The repo is the research log; the portfolio shows the distilled logs. Follow along as the bench grows.
highlights: Linear algebra, calculus and probability from axioms
Forward and backward pass in pure NumPy
Backpropagation derived by hand — no autograd
Optimisers from SGD to Adam, built step by step
Now: CNNs, attention, Transformers

faq.a: Daily since 1 July 2026 — the mission is 548 days to 31 Dec 2027. Each day is a notebook.

faq.q: Do you use PyTorch or pure NumPy?
faq.a: Both — I first build everything in pure NumPy by hand (backprop, Adam, CNN), then show the PyTorch version for comparison.
Yes — clone hariomlohardev/AGI_Research, open any notebook in Jupyter, and run top to bottom. No API keys needed.

projects.name: micrograd_hk
projects.description: A tiny autograd engine on NumPy — a Value graph with vectorised backprop and gradient descent, written before touching a framework. Inspired by micrograd, but matrix-driven: pip install micrograd_hk, Colab demo included.
projects.longDescription:
A tiny autograd engine built on NumPy for fast, matrix-driven backpropagation — the from-scratch work of the AGI notebook, packaged so anyone can install it.

It implements a minimal `Value` computation graph, inspired by [karpathy/micrograd](https://github.com/karpathy/micrograd), but where micrograd differentiates scalar by scalar, this one vectorises every operation over full NumPy matrices — so training is significantly faster. `@`, `+`, `-`, `**`, `sum` and `tanh` all carry a backward pass.

On top of the engine sit a small `DenseLayer` / `MLP` API and a `Trainer` with automatic checkpointing and five optimisers: SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, Adam, and **Adam-M** — a modified Adam derived and tuned as part of this project.

```bash
pip install micrograd_hk
```

```python
from micrograd_hk import Value, DenseLayer, MLP, Trainer

m = MLP(shape=[1, 3], nouts=[8, 8, 1])
trainer = Trainer(m, xs_matrix, ys_matrix)
final_loss, y_pred = trainer.train(lr=0.01, iterations=3000, optimizer="adam_m")
```

There is a runnable [Colab demo](https://colab.research.google.com/github/hariomlohardev/micrograd-hk/blob/main/demo.ipynb) if you would rather read it than install it. MIT licensed, Python 3.8+.
highlights: Matrix-first `Value` autograd engine with a full backward pass
Vectorised over NumPy matrices, not scalar by scalar
`DenseLayer` and `MLP` building blocks
Five optimisers: SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, Adam and a custom Adam-M
`Trainer` with automatic checkpoint save and load
Written before touching PyTorch — the maths first, the framework after

faq.q: How is this different from micrograd?
faq.a: micrograd differentiates one scalar at a time. micrograd_hk keeps the same minimal Value graph but vectorises every operation over NumPy matrices, so a network trains in a fraction of the time while the code stays readable.
A modified Adam developed and tuned inside this project, selected with optimizer="adam_m". SGD, Momentum, RMSProp and standard Adam ship alongside it.

faq.q: Can I try it without installing anything?
faq.a: Yes — open demo.ipynb in Colab from the repo badge and run it top to bottom.

projects.name: peek
projects.description: htop for codebases — understand any repo in five seconds. Languages, size and structure in one screen: pip install peek-code && peek .
projects.longDescription:
A zero-config codebase cartographer. Point it at any repository and it draws the map: languages, size, structure and the files that actually matter — in about five seconds, entirely offline.

```bash
pip install peek-code
peek .
```

The default is an interactive TUI built on Rich and Textual — `j/k` to move, `/` to filter, `o` to open a file in `$EDITOR`, `enter` for details. `peek --no-tui` prints a static Rich report for screenshots, pipes and CI, and `peek --html -o map.html` writes a shareable page.

Two commands go further than a summary. `peek --pack` selects the highest-signal files within a token budget and prints them as one LLM-ready bundle — `peek --pack --ask "auth"` narrows it to a topic. `peek trace` walks a function tree across files: what calls it, what it calls, and how deep, with `--html` for a browsable version.

```bash
peek find "token validation" . --limit 10
peek trace scan --depth 3 --html
```

Python 3.11+, ten themes, 146 tests, MIT. Issues tagged **good first issue** are open if you want to build on it.
highlights: Read any codebase in about five seconds, fully offline
Interactive TUI, static Rich output, or a shareable HTML map
`--pack` builds an LLM-ready bundle inside a token budget
`peek find` ranks matches across filenames and content
`peek trace` walks the function tree across files, with an HTML view
Ten themes, 146 passing tests, zero configuration

faq.q: What does peek do that `ls` or `cloc` does not?
faq.a: It answers the question you actually have about an unfamiliar repo: what is this, which language dominates, where does the code live, and which files should I read first — in one screen instead of five commands.

faq.q: Does it send my code anywhere?
faq.a: No. Everything runs locally and works offline. The optional `--llm` summary is the only feature that talks to an API, and it stays off unless you set a key yourself.
Yes — the repo keeps a set of issues labelled good first issue. Install with pip install -e "./peek[dev]" and the test suite runs locally.

projects.name: inkdown
projects.description: Notion for Markdown — write in a clean editor, ship plain .md files. Local-first desktop app: no account, no lock-in.
projects.longDescription:
A Markdown studio that feels like a modern notes app and leaves behind nothing but plain `.md` files. Local-first, offline, no account, no telemetry — your notes stay on your disk.

The library side handles multiple files and folders, search, archive and import from a file, a URL or the clipboard. The editor gives live preview, split and focus modes, a table of contents, a minimap and a word goal, with syntax highlighting for 180+ languages, KaTeX maths, mermaid diagrams, callouts and footnotes.

Past writing, it adds day-based todos with a desktop widget and a streak, slide decks built straight from `##` headings with speaker notes, five-colour highlights, version history, a `Ctrl+P` command palette, and export to Markdown, HTML, PDF, PNG or a zip.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/hariomlohardev/inkdown && cd inkdown
pip install -r requirements.txt
python main.py
```

Built with PyWebView and vanilla JavaScript — Python 3.11+. Windows gets a one-click installer from Releases; any OS can run the web preview. MIT licensed.
highlights: Plain `.md` files in, plain `.md` files out — no proprietary format
Live preview with split, focus, TOC, minimap and a word goal
180+ languages highlighted, plus KaTeX, mermaid, callouts and footnotes
Day-based todos with a desktop widget, streak and quick capture
Slides generated from `##` headings, with speaker notes
100% local and offline — no account, no telemetry

faq.a: On your machine, as ordinary Markdown files alongside a local inkdown-data.json. Nothing is uploaded and there is no account to create.
Windows gets a one-click installer from Releases. On any other OS you can run it from source with Python 3.11+, or open the web preview with npx serve app.

faq.q: What happens if I stop using it?
faq.a: You keep your files. Everything is standard Markdown, so any other editor opens it — that is the point of shipping .md instead of a database.

projects.name: practice_code

projects.longDescription:
60+ Python solutions for algorithms and data structures, grouped by topic — arrays, strings, trees, graphs, DP, and more. Each solution notes time and space complexity.

Fork-friendly: add your approach in any language, keep the same folder structure, and open a PR. Built to stay readable and interview-ready.
highlights: 60+ problems with complexity notes
Grouped by topic: arrays, trees, graphs, DP
Fork-friendly — add your solution

faq.q: What language are the solutions in?
faq.a: Python — clean, commented, with complexity noted at the top of each file.

faq.q: Can I add solutions in other languages?
faq.a: Yes — fork, add a parallel folder for your language, keep the problem naming, and open a PR.
Yes — classic DSA patterns grouped by topic so you can drill arrays, trees, graphs or DP in order.
